title: Out Loud
logline: A correction sent after a morning of drafts, a reply that takes all day, a grandmother on the stairs — and coffee at an hour nobody keeps, the night before everyone goes home.

previously.text: In Montecito a girl in a window seat had Flannery O’Connor exactly backwards. You crossed the room yourself.
Soaking wet on the sand at Ellery Beach she said, “I’d like to kiss you now.” You kissed her before she finished.
She typed herself into your phone — SKYE (MISFIT). You asked her last name. “Out.”
In the basement Lena played “Clair de lune” properly, around the dead F. “The last time I played it right in front of anybody was in November. Four years ago.”
At halftime you asked Theo home to Youngstown. He said yes before you finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. “Guests bring something.”
You came home at six in the morning, soaked and humming. Theo: “Where’d you go?” “Argued about a book till it got light.” “Of course you did.”

body: The only light in 412 is the one inside the RAZR. Jack is holding it open over his face at the end of an arm that went to sleep around six, and past it, over Theo’s desk, the window is starting to have things in it: the eucalyptus along the Lagoon first, black on a lesser black, then the sky letting itself in behind the trees a shade at a time. He got in from the Saturday close at twenty past one and slept till five. Since five he has been on his back on his own bed with the phone open to SKYE (MISFIT), in her capitals.
In the lot she switched the guessing off so she could spell her own name. At five he switched it back on, because one letter at a time would take him till Thanksgiving.
*hi its jack.* Deleted. She typed herself into this phone and called herself from it. She knows who it is.
*about last night* — that’s how you start a confession, or a country song, and he doesn’t want to be in either one. Deleted.

*thanks for the* — and then the 5, the 4, the 7, the 7. The RAZR, guessing, offers him a word. He presses down on the little silver pad and it offers him the other word that lives on the same four keys. He shuts the phone on both of them like it bit him, and lies there with it closed on his breastbone.

When he opens it again he types *the grandmother*, and that one he keeps. He knows what he wants to say: she was wrong. He has known it since the den, since LIAR down a margin in Sharpie, and he has the argument — he had it Friday, he had it again last night at the Anchor sink with his arms in the rinse water — and it’s a good argument, and it runs about four pages. Jack Costigan, who will argue with anybody about anything at two in the morning for the pleasure of it, cannot get being right into a hundred and sixty characters. Every word he takes out is a word he needs. He takes them out anyway. *the grandmother* sits on the little screen with the cursor blinking after it, waiting on the rest.
At twenty to seven the door opens and Theo comes in.

His khakis are wet to the shin, and above the wet they’re crusted with sand, and his loafers have gone dark with the sea. He’s carrying a gas-station coffee in a paper cup with the lid on. His hair is perfect.
“You’re up,” Theo says.
“You’re out.”
Theo takes the lid off the coffee, blows across it, and puts the lid back on. “I run now.”
His eyes go to the phone open in Jack’s hand. Jack shuts it.

Theo says nothing, at volume. He sets the coffee on the desk by the MacBook, steps out of the loafers where he stands, and lies down on his bed with his sandy ankles crossed and his hands folded on his chest.

The coffee steams on the desk. The window is light enough to read by now. After a minute Jack turns on his side toward the wall and opens the RAZR again under the edge of the blanket, where the light won’t carry to Theo’s side of the room, and the cursor is still blinking after *the grandmother*.

body.text: 10–0 or bust. Sully’s at ten. Bring your Browns face. —L.

body: Sully’s has three televisions going and two that matter. The big screen over the bar has the Saints in Tampa. The tube in the corner has the Browns in Detroit, and under it, on his stool at the end of the bar, is Dale Wisniewski in the Barry Sanders jersey with a stack of quarters by his glass. His Lions went oh and sixteen last year. He has been there since they unlocked the door. The third set has the Steelers in Kansas City, and nobody at Sully’s has an opinion about it but the bartender.

Lena has the chair under the bell, in black and gold, with the rope tied off to its cleat at her elbow and a Kleenex up her sleeve. Friday’s cold has gone down into her chest and left her a voice like a gravel road. Julian has pulled a stool up beside her chair, in a cardigan, learning: he watches the snap, and then he watches Lena to find out whether it was good.

“Laney gave me your message,” she tells Jack when he sits down. “I was ahead of you. I ate it cold, out of the quart, standing at the sill at six in the morning.” She aims a finger at him. “Don’t you dare tell Gloria.”

Laney is in sunglasses at ten in the morning and has said good morning to nobody. She’s looking under the table, at Jack’s boots. Every time he shifts his feet a little more of Ellery Beach comes out of the welts onto Sully’s floorboards.
“Fireman,” Laney says, “why is there a *beach* in your boots?”
Then the Saints break the huddle, and she turns back to the screen before he has to have an answer.

Kevin drove. He keeps score on a bar napkin with a golf pencil, both games in two neat columns. Theo is asleep in 412. On the fourth chair, where Becca sat last week with her celery, there’s Laney’s purse.
“Where’s her saint?” Dale asks the bartender, looking along the bar for St. Jude. Lena answers for him, in the gravel. “He has limits, Dale.”

It’s seven all after a quarter, and Lena sits forward on the chair with both fists on her knees. Then the Saints score, and score again, and keep scoring — thirty-one points in a row — and every time, the owner unties the rope and Lena stands up on the rung and rings it and does a WHO DAT that comes out mostly gravel.
Between series the RAZR is open under the table, below the edge, with *the grandmother* on it and nothing after.
Lena catches him at it once. “Who’re you texting?”
“No one.”
She looks at him over the Kleenex until Brees is throwing again, and lets him have it.

In the corner, meanwhile, Brady Quinn is throwing touchdown passes, which a Browns quarterback isn’t supposed to be able to do. Jack, who buried Quinn in this same bar on Monday, with full honors, starts exhuming him a drive at a time. The second touchdown he calls a clerical error. The third, a sign. Lena, between Saints scores, tells him the Saints once went three and thirteen in a city that wasn’t theirs and she watched every snap, and asks whether he’d like a tissue for his hope.
Kevin, who doesn’t follow the Browns, leans across with the golf pencil. “Is this good? Your face says it’s bad.”
“It’s good,” Jack says. “That’s why my face says it’s bad.”
Quinn throws a fourth, and Jack, who was raised to know better, lets himself hope. The Browns lose on the last play of the game, thirty-eight to thirty-seven.

Dale comes off his stool with both arms over his head. Then he turns around and sees Jack’s face, and he brings his arms down and sits back on the stool and lifts a finger to the bartender, and a root beer comes sliding down the bar.
“Told you,” Dale says. “A tragedy either way.” He raises his own glass to Jack. “You’re the only man in California who knows what that cost.”
And Jack, whose team has just lost a football game on the last play, lifts the root beer back down the bar to Dale and finds he can’t stop grinning.
Lena has been watching him grin. “You look like something happened to you.”
“Ohio State beat Michigan.”
“That was *yesterday*.”
“It’s still happening to me.”
She narrows her eyes at him. Julian asks her about a yellow flag on the big screen, and she turns to answer him.

With four minutes left the Bucs are throwing on every down, and the Saints send an extra defensive back trotting onto the field, and Julian, who has been told twice, leans across Lena’s chair. “Sorry. The nickel,” he says to Jack. “What is it, again?”

journal.text: Dale Wisniewski. A Lions fan alone at the end of Sully’s bar in a Barry Sanders jersey. Warren, Michigan — not the other one. Tips in quarters. Said the rookie’s going to be good. Lions 38, Browns 37, on the last play. He bought me a root beer: the only man in California who knows what that cost.

choices.text: “Five DBs. You bring one in when they go three wide.”
response: “Five DBs,” Jack says. “You bring one in when they go three wide.” And then, because that isn’t an explanation, he does it properly, the way his father did it for him in the garage on Glenwood: the ketchup bottle is the quarterback, two coasters are the corners, and his root beer is the fifth defensive back, coming on for a linebacker. Julian gets it on the third try. “Okay. *Okay*,” he says, and thanks him.
Up on the chair, with the Kleenex at her nose, Lena watches Jack explain football to her boyfriend with a bottle of Heinz.
The clock runs out in Tampa. Thirty-eight to seven. Ten and oh.

“I’m crying,” Julian says.
“Good,” says Lena. “That’s how you learn.”

s03.slug: SUNDAY · 1:35 PM · THE ANACAPA LOT, KEVIN’S ODYSSEY
body: Lena carried the polish out of Sully’s in her coat pocket like a flask. Now she’s at the Odyssey’s back bumper in the first real sun since Thursday, her voice down to about half of itself, and across the back glass, in the white La Vang car-wash polish, WHO DAT · 9–0 has gone streaky with a week of fog. The 9 is hers: fat on top and leaning into the next number, the way only she makes them.
“My nine,” she says. “I’ll take it down.” She does it herself, with the remover and a corner of the Kleenex, and steps back from a window that now says WHO DAT · –0. It reads like a threat.

Kevin has the keys and his backpack and somewhere to be. “Library. Orgo doesn’t care that we’re ten and oh. Make it legible — I park this thing in front of the Brick.” Julian stands at Lena’s elbow with his hands in his cardigan pockets, reading the glass with real attention. Eight days in, he has stopped asking what WHO DAT means and started saying it under his breath.

“She made me practice the chant in the car,” he tells Jack. “I’m told I’m flat.” “He’s a tenor,” Lena says. “Tenors can’t holler. It’s a known thing.” Jack has his hands in the Carhartt and, in one of them, a phone with a sentence in it he hasn’t sent.
Lena wipes the neck of the bottle on her jeans and holds it out. “Your turn, Youngstown.”

choices.text: Write the ten yourself.
response: He takes the bottle. The 1 goes on fine. The 0 starts out round, gets ambitious, and ends up an egg leaning hard to the left, with a drip of polish running off the bottom of it.
“That,” Lena says, hoarse and enormously pleased with him, “is the worst ten I have ever seen. In my *life*. Give it a flag. It needs something to hold it up.”
He draws a fleur-de-lis beside it. It comes out looking like a fork. She studies the fork, sniffs, and lets it stand.
Then they scatter: Lena into Julian’s car with her Kleenex, Kevin into the Odyssey with the ten still wet on the glass, backing out slow so it won’t run. Jack stays in the lot.

choices.text: Hand it to Julian. “He should do the ten. He’s learning.”
response: “He should do the ten,” Jack says, and passes the bottle across. “He’s learning.”

Julian checks with Lena, who says nothing at all, so he steps up to the glass. He writes it in a composer’s hand — the 1 a clean stem, the 0 closed at the top, the two of them the same height and properly spaced, neat as a score. Then he caps the bottle.
Lena reads the ten. “Perfect,” she says, to Jack, and puts the remover back in her pocket without looking at him.
Then they scatter: Lena into Julian’s car with her Kleenex, Kevin into the Odyssey with the ten still wet on the glass, backing out slow so it won’t run. Jack stays in the lot.

choices.text: “You do it. I’m in mourning.”
response: “You do it,” Jack says. “I’m in mourning.”
“I’m not letting you near a ten either,” Lena says, already uncapping it. “I’ve seen your eights.”
She writes the ten herself, big, a flag on the 1 and the 0 shaded down one side for depth. “Thirty-seven points and you lost,” she tells him over her shoulder. “That’s not mourning. That’s Ohio.”
Then they scatter: Lena into Julian’s car with her Kleenex, Kevin into the Odyssey with the ten still wet on the glass, backing out slow so it won’t run. Jack stays in the lot.

s03a.slug: SUNDAY · 1:48 PM · THE ANACAPA LOT, THE WALL BY THE BIKE RACKS
body: The low wall by the bike racks is cinderblock with a concrete cap, and by a quarter to two it has taken in enough sun to be warm through his jeans. Somebody’s U-lock hangs open on the nearest rack. Across the lot a gull is working the lid of a dumpster with total confidence and no results.

He hasn’t been properly warm since he walked into the Pacific on Friday night. He keeps finding the beach on him — in the seam of his jeans, in the eyelets of his boots, a few grains at the bottom of the Carhartt’s pocket, in with his keys.

Jack sits on the wall with the RAZR open on his knee — SKYE (MISFIT), where she typed herself in — and the sentence he has been carrying around since the den, through a Saints rout and a Lions miracle and Dale’s root beer.

It started out long. It started out Aquinas-long, with objections and replies: that the grandmother isn’t working an angle at the end; that every con wants something, and the hand on the Misfit’s shoulder wants nothing; that a girl who listens to how people breathe ought to be able to hear the difference; that he can prove it, with page numbers. On T9 that’s four hundred key presses and a commitment. So he takes words out. He takes out the page numbers, and the breathing, and the hand. He takes out everything he would say to Hale. What’s left fits on the little screen, and it’s all bone.
She has the number. It gets signed anyway; that’s half the joke. And it starts *misfit*, because that’s what he called her, and she boxed it. That part was never in doubt.
She crossed out CON in her own capitals. He wants it in writing that she meant it.
He has it three ways.

s04.slug: SUNDAY · 3:10 PM · THE BRICK → DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL
body: The third-floor reading room of the Brick makes the sound a hundred people make trying not to make any: radiators knocking under the tall windows, a stapler going somewhere back in the stacks, a page turned carefully, so as not to wake anybody. Outside, the Sunday campus is going home early for the week, roller bags clattering down the path toward the lots. Jack has a long table to himself and a yellow legal pad, and across the top of the first page, in his small square capitals, Hale’s question: WHETHER A PROMISE BINDS WHEN ITS REASON IS GONE. Under it, because Hale assigned it to him: NO.

He argues it for eight pages. A promise is a tool, he writes, made for a job; when the job is gone, the man who goes on keeping it isn’t faithful, he’s only loyal to his own handwriting. Hume says something like it — that the obligation of a promise is an invention, a convention men keep because it pays them — and around four o’clock, with Hume open at his elbow, Jack writes the best paragraph he has written all semester. He doesn’t believe a word of it.
The RAZR lies face down beside the legal pad, where he put it.

choices.text: Leave it face down till Mass.
response: He leaves it there, face down, through Hume and the conclusion and the footnotes.
By half past five it’s dark out. He prints it in the basement, eight pages at a dime a page, and carries it home across the Commons still warm.

At twenty past eight the Fishbowl TV has the American Music Awards on, and Laney is on the couch under it between two of her Pi Lam sisters with a bag of kettle corn. On the screen a girl in a sequined dress stands at a microphone looking astonished to be there; a woman goes by in a headdress made of light.
Laney addresses the television. “Taylor Swift is going to win everything there is,” she says, “and she’s *still* going to be nicer than me.”
“Everybody’s nicer than you,” one of the sisters says.
“That’s what I *said*.” Laney holds the kettle corn up over the back of the couch without looking, and Jack, on his way through with eight pages and a blazer to find before Mass, takes a handful.
“Mass?” she says, without turning around.
“Nine o’clock.”
“Light a candle for Kanye,” Laney says. “Taylor’s going to be nice to him till he dies.”

s05.music: The St. Brendan’s Choir — “To Jesus Christ, Our Sovereign King”
body: Christ the King comes in cold. Somebody has propped the doors for the stragglers, and the night off Ocean Road comes up the center aisle to meet the incense halfway. For the last Sunday of the Church’s year the organist has come to the nine o’clock himself, and the guitars are sitting this one out in their cases against the sacristy wall. He takes the entrance hymn at full organ — a hymn written for a cathedral and a thousand voices — and the hundred or so students under the hull of St. Brendan’s do what they can to be a thousand. Father Osei comes up the aisle behind the cross in white and gold, with the little hitch in his step, smiling up at the ceiling like the hymn is a joke he’s been let in on.

Jack has the end of the fourth pew on the right. Lena is beside him in the black mantilla with a roll of cough drops in her lap, and beside her is Julian, in a cardigan, who has most of the responses now. Tonight Lena is down to a whisper, so he says them for the pair of them, a little behind the room, and she mouths along with him. Across the aisle, the fourth pew on the left is full of nursing students.

Kenzie Rourke sings the psalm from the ambo — *The Lord is king; he is robed in majesty* — and on the refrain Lena’s mouth moves and nothing comes out of it but air. Julian, without looking over, sings it a little louder.

The RAZR is on silent in the front pocket of his jeans. Once, during the second reading — *Behold, he is coming amid the clouds* — he feels it go against his leg, and puts his hand over the pocket, and it hasn’t. He keeps his hand there anyway, till the Alleluia.

Father Osei reads the Gospel himself: Pilate in his headquarters, asking a prisoner whether he is a king, and the prisoner answering some other question. *Everyone who belongs to the truth listens to my voice.* That’s where it stops.

Osei comes down to the step without notes. “Pilate’s next line, which we did not read tonight, is ‘What is truth?’ — and he asks it with the Truth standing in front of him, close enough to touch. Most of us ask it the same way, my friends, with our backs half turned.” He sits down. Near the back, a baby has a remark to make about that.
In the quiet after Communion, on the kneeler, he says *Becca* once into his folded hands. A week of it left.

Then he gives God what he has: Nonna, still sleeping in the front-room chair so she won’t have to manage the stairs; his father in the garage with the last play of a football game; Gina, who sleeps through first period; Danny, where it’s already midnight. He doesn’t bring up Friday night. He wouldn’t know how to start it, or what he’d be asking for, and he kneels there not knowing until Lena’s elbow tells him it’s time to sit.
The last hymn of the year is the King’s again, the organist pulling out everything he has left, and Lena, who has no voice at all, sings it anyway, an octave under where she means to be, every verse.

s06.slug: SUNDAY · 10:05 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE COURTYARD WALL
body: By ten the cold has settled into the courtyard for the night: into the flagstones, into the low wall under the olive tree, into the broken sprinkler that somebody finally shut off at the valve, so the lake that used to stand under the tree has dried to a crust of mud with leaves set in it. A fat crescent moon is going down yellow behind the Grove. Through the A-frame’s door, propped open with a hymnal, the organ starts something, stops in the middle and starts it again. Julian is in there with the organist, asking about the organ. He has been asking for twenty minutes, and the organist, by the sound of it, has been waiting thirty years for somebody to.

Lena is on the wall with her coat buttoned to the chin and a fresh box of Kleenex in her lap, the lotion kind. Jack is beside her. The cold has made her nose red and her eyes bright, and she is beautiful with a cold. It isn’t fair, and it isn’t his business. Her voice has gone down another notch since the bar. “Osei,” she says, to start, “has a dirty trick of sitting down two sentences before you’re ready.” Then she spends what’s left of her voice on Hale.
“It’s due at nine,” she says, “and it’s *good*, and I’m furious about it. You want my thesis?”
“No.”

“*A promise is made to a person, not to a reason.*” One finger up, like she’s calling a point of order. “*When the reason goes, the person is still standing there.*” Then she blows her nose and spoils it, and doesn’t care. “That’s page one. The rest is footnotes and me being right.”
“I argued the other side.”
“I know you did. Hale made you.” She turns her head against the cold to look at him. “Did you convince yourself?”
“I convinced the paper.”

“That is the saddest thing anybody has ever said to me on this wall,” she says, “and you did the Nebraska cow on this wall.” She shifts the box on her knees. “Go on, then. Argue the other side at me. I have to hear it before nine.”
“And if the person doesn’t want it kept anymore?”
“Then they let you off it. They say so, to your face. That’s the only door out.” She points the Kleenex at him. “You don’t get to decide it *for* them. That’s the paper. That’s page six.”
She takes that in herself, and looks out at the olive tree. “I was supposed to prove the thing I least believe,” she says. “I think I talked myself into it. Hale would be unbearable about it.”
She tucks the Kleenex box under one arm. “Have you told your mama yet?” “Tomorrow.” “*Still?*” “Tomorrow.”
Inside, the organ goes up into something enormous and stops dead. In the quiet after it, Lena picks at the cardboard edge of the box.
“You had a beach in your boots this morning.”

response: “Theo dragged me to a party,” Jack says. “In Montecito.”

“Good,” Lena says. “You needed dragging.” She nods, satisfied with Theo, and then she’s on to Hale — whether he’ll grade the two of them on the same curve, whether Hale has ever in his life graded on a curve or only on grudges — and she never comes back around to Montecito.

The organ stops for good. Julian comes out through the propped door with his car keys already in his hand and his cardigan buttoned wrong by one, and says, “Goodnight, Jack,” and means it. Lena gets down off the wall. “Nine o’clock,” she tells Jack. “Pigeonhole. Be late and I win by default.” Then the two of them cross the courtyard to Ocean Road, and Jack is still on the wall when the organist comes out after them with a ring of keys the size of a tambourine, locks up St. Brendan’s for the night, and tells Jack, unasked, that the young man knows his stops.

Lena answers the curve: Hale doesn’t grade on a curve, Hale grades on grudges, and she has been building one with him on purpose since September. She answers Mémère’s cold, which Mémère claims she caught off Lena over the telephone on Friday, out of solidarity, and is treating with a novena and a little whiskey. She answers her flight, Wednesday, at an hour she says God Himself hasn’t seen. And she doesn’t ask again.

She doesn’t ask. She reaches up and takes her paper out of his hand, which has started to crush it, folds it once and pushes it into the inside pocket of the Carhartt, flat against his chest. Then she holds up his. “Call her,” she says. “I’ll keep yours warm.”

He doesn’t call from the steps. The signal on the steps comes and goes, and he isn’t going to lose his mother to it. He walks to Delgado, and then he runs, all the way up the east stairs to the fourth-floor landing, where it holds. He gets most of a Hail Mary said between two and four. He dials with his back to the cinderblock.

It’s quarter past five on Glenwood Avenue. His mother picks up before the first ring has finished, from the kitchen, and she has gone calm, the way she does in hospitals. He can hear the nylon of her coat every time she moves the phone.

“She’s okay. Listen to me first. She’s okay.” Then the rest, in order, the way she’d give it to the school nurse. Nonna went up the stairs this afternoon — the stairs she has been sleeping in the front-room chair for two weeks to keep off — because she wanted her good rosary from the dresser, the one from San Giovanni. She had decided God could tell the difference. She got the rosary. She came down the fast way.

He knows those stairs. Fourteen of them, steep, under the brown runner Nonna picked out herself, with the seventh tread that complains no matter where you step on it; he carried her laundry up them from the time he was ten so she wouldn’t have to.
Gina found her at the bottom when she got in from Ursuline, and called the ambulance, and went out to the garage for her father.

“Gina did everything right,” his mother says. “Fifteen years old, and she did every single thing right, Jack — the towel, the ambulance, my number, your father — and now she’s up in her room with the door shut and she won’t come down. Text her later. Not now. Later.”

“A broken wrist. Six stitches over the eye. And they’re keeping her at St. Elizabeth’s for her heart — a monitor, for the dizzy spells. They want to see what it does at night. She’s *stable*, that’s their word.” A breath. “She told the paramedic he was handsome. Then she wouldn’t get in his ambulance. She said she’d go with Frank.” Another breath, and something that might be a laugh if it were any other day. “And I’m to tell Giacomino it wasn’t the stairs. She was in a hurry, and the rosary wasn’t.”
“Pop drove her?”
“Your father drove her. He was sober, Jack. I want you to know that. He carried her out to the truck himself.”
Somebody picks up the extension in the front hall. “She asked for you,” his father says. “Then she asked about the Browns.” “Thirty-seven points, Pop.” “And we lose.” Click.
“I can get a bus tonight. The paper’s in.”

“You will not. Wednesday is soon enough.” A cupboard; the clink of a pill bottle going into a bag. “You’ve got your paper.” “I turned it in, Ma.” “Then you’ve got another one. You always have another one. She’d get up out of that bed and kill you.”
“And Theo’s still coming?”
“Wednesday. He bought plane tickets.”
“*Plane* tickets.” She takes a moment over the price of them. “Madonna. Does he eat? Your father says he’s all bones and a wristwatch.”
“He eats, Ma.”
“He’ll eat here.”
“And your friend? The girl. Lena.” “She’s going home, Ma. New Orleans.” “Of course she is. Her mother’d want her.”

body.title: M. Broussard — PHIL 9H — YES
body.text:
WHETHER A PROMISE BINDS WHEN ITS REASON IS GONE: YES

A promise is made to a person, not to a reason. When the reason goes, the person is still standing there.

. . .

Take Ruth, since the other side won’t. By the end of the first chapter every reason she had is buried in Moab: the husband, his brother, his father, any hope of sons. Naomi says so herself, in the road, and tells both her daughters-in-law to go home. That is the only honest door out of a promise: the person it was made to, opening it, to your face. Naomi holds it open with both hands. Orpah kisses her and goes, and Scripture doesn’t say one unkind word about Orpah, and neither will I. Ruth won’t go. *Quocumque perrexeris, pergam.* She isn’t confused about the facts. She has buried the facts. She has only noticed the one that’s left, which is that Naomi is still standing in the road. The reasons were never what she promised. They were only why. (p. 5)

s14.slug: TUESDAY · 12:10 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S → THE GROVE
body: Father Osei says the 12:10 in red. The martyrs of Vietnam, a hundred and seventeen of them; he gives them one sentence before the Gloria — bishops and priests and catechists, and two soldiers who were ordered to walk across a crucifix and wouldn’t — and then a second: “Some of us will not walk across the quad for Him. Pray for us also.” A dozen people sit in the blue light under the hull, and at the ends of three of the pews there are roller bags parked with their handles up. Somewhere in San Jose, Kevin said this morning, his mother reads eleven of the names.

Jack caught Osei at the sacristy door before Mass with an index card. Osei read it once, put it inside his book, and gripped Jack’s arm above the elbow, a doctor’s grip, and by the time he let go the entrance hymn had started, so Jack took the last pew on the right rather than walk up the aisle in the middle of it. Lena is in the fourth pew on the right, alone, with her bag on the end. Across the aisle, in the fourth on the left, Becca kneels beside Joey Abruzzo.
At the Prayers of the Faithful Osei does the Church and the Pope, the persecuted, and everybody who will be on the roads and in the air this week. Then he opens the book and takes out the card.
“For Carmela Rinaldi,” he reads, “in the hospital in Youngstown, Ohio.”
“Lord, hear our prayer,” say eleven people and Jack.

Her name goes up under the hull along with the Pope’s. Across the aisle Becca’s head comes up out of her hands. And Lena, who has known since yesterday afternoon, turns around in her pew anyway, all the way around, and looks for him in the back, and keeps him until Osei has moved on to the dead. She faces the altar again.

The Grove after Mass is eucalyptus bark lying across the path in long curls, and the smell the trees give off when the sun has been on them since ten. Lena waits for him under them with the LG open in her hand. Her voice is most of the way back, with a crack still running down the middle of it.

“Mémère called at seven,” she says. “She’s lighting a candle for your nonna. Tonight, at St. Bernard’s, after the rosary. But she wants the whole name.” And then, in Mémère’s French: “*La moitié d’un nom, c’est la moitié d’une chandelle.* Half a name is half a candle. I tried to tell her Carmela was plenty. She said, Carmela *what*.”
“Carmela Rinaldi,” Jack says.

Lena types it with both thumbs on the little keyboard, letter by letter, into a text to her Tante Claudine in Lafayette, who has the job of driving Mémère to St. Bernard’s and holding the lighter. She reads it back to him to be sure, *Carmela Rinaldi*, in a New Orleans that does things to the vowels Nonna would object to and then forgive.
“And she says your nonna raised a boy with manners,” Lena adds, sending it, “so she’s owed.”
“Who drove her?” “My dad.” He gives it a breath. “Sober.” “Good,” Lena says — and nothing else.
Her flight is first thing tomorrow. Julian is driving her. “He says he likes airports at that hour,” she says. “I told him that’s a character flaw, and I’d pray for him.”

Down the path Becca comes out of St. Brendan’s side door with her clipboard on her hip, headed for Portolá. She lifts a hand to them, small, and keeps going. Lena waves back big, with the phone still in it.

It buzzes in her hand before Becca is out of sight. Lena reads it and laughs, crack and all, and turns the screen so he can see Tante Claudine’s answer: *Done. Mama says Carmela goes ahead of the Saints’ secondary. That is an honor. Last year it was the levees.*

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle.

s16.slug: WEDNESDAY · 1:05 AM · THE WHARF → THE 101 NORTH
body: The Wharf Rat’s sign has said WHARF RAT in pink neon since before Jack was born, and these days only the RAT holds steady; the WHARF comes and goes. Past it the boards run on another hundred feet over the black water, past the bait shack and the fish-cleaning sink, out beyond the last of the light from the Anchor’s windows, and down at the very end a car is idling with its top up and one taillight laying a little red on the planks.

Jack comes down the wharf at five past one with his apron stuffed in his back pocket and La Flaca left chained to the rail behind the Anchor to wait out Thanksgiving, his hands still pruned from six hours of the Hobart, and Gloria’s white box held out in front of him by the string so nothing inside it shifts. He can hear the tape deck before he gets there — Stevie Nicks at a murmur through the canvas, the same side of the same album. Before he reaches the car she leans across from the driver’s seat and shoves his door open from inside.
“Coat check,” she says.

She has on a different flannel, green and black and big enough for two of her, and nothing at all on her feet. He gets in with the box on his knees and watches her find the clutch barefoot. She looks tired around the eyes in a way she didn’t on Friday, and wide awake everywhere else.
“How was work?”

“Work,” she says, and becomes it. She plucks three pins out of the corner of her mouth that aren’t there, sets them back between her teeth, and talks around them from somewhere in the old country by way of Burbank — “Arms up. Down. You ate a sandwich since Thursday, I can tell, I am not angry, I am only telling you” — and then she’s the girl inside the dress, standing very still on a box with her chin up, apologizing to a hem. Back and forth, the woman and the girl, until the woman gets the last pin in and the girl says “Ow” in a very small voice. Then the pins go back wherever she keeps them.
“Since ten this morning,” she says. “I drove up after. I’ve been back two hours. I took a shower and lay on the floor.” She glances down at his lap. “What’s in the box?”
“My grandmother’s pie.”

Her eyes stay on the box a little longer — the white cardboard, Gloria’s red-and-white string knotted twice, before she puts the car in gear and rolls them up the wharf with the headlights off until they’re past the Anchor’s windows.
“Not the diner you work at,” she says. “I’m not eating pie in front of your boss.”

Mission Street is dark from the water to the freeway. At the on-ramp the all-night place sits under its own tall sign with every window blazing, a yellow box with a cop at the counter and three cars out front and a busboy mopping in the middle of all that light. Skye slows, and looks at it, and doesn’t turn in.
“Too bright,” she says, and takes the ramp north.
“Where, then?”
“Twenty minutes. Somewhere nobody I know has ever been.”

The 101 runs along the water for a few miles past the last of the town, the sea on their left darker than the sky and the railroad keeping it company, and then the highway turns its back on the ocean and starts to climb, up through a cut in the hills where the dark gets bigger and the trucks get slower, their running lights strung up the grade ahead of them like beads off a broken rosary.

s17.slug: WEDNESDAY · 1:30 AM · THE STARLITE, A TRUCK STOP ON THE 101
body: The Starlite smells of coffee that has been on the burner since the last shift change, diesel off the islands, and something sugary going dark on a griddle. It sits at the top of the grade, where the trucks pull off to breathe: six diesel islands under sodium lamps the color of weak tea, a gravel apron where the eighteen-wheelers park nose to tail and idle in their sleep, and a long low building from 1958 that nobody has ever had the money to ruin. Out front, on a pole taller than the building, a neon star with five points, two of them dead, so that from the highway it looks like a star that lost a fight and stayed open anyway.

Inside there’s a coffee counter with stools bolted to the floor and boomerangs in the Formica, a rack of cassettes and beef jerky by the register, a hand-lettered card taped to the cash drawer — SHOWERS · DRIVERS · $8 · ASK — and through an archway a back room of red leatherette booths, patched here and there with red tape. Four men sit along the counter in caps and canvas coats that have done more work than the Carhartt ever will, each with his own sugar pourer and his own silence. The night waitress wears BEV on her name tag and is somewhere in her sixties, with her hair up in a clip and a pencil stuck through it. She takes in the two of them — a barefoot girl, and a boy carrying a pie into a place that sells pie — and says, “You kids sit anywhere,” and means the back.

There’s a jukebox in the archway, a Seeburg with its chrome gone milky. Skye feeds it a quarter before she does anything else and punches in a number without bothering with the cards, and by the time they’re sliding into a booth by the window, Mazzy Star is coming out of it slow and underwater: a slide guitar, a tambourine somebody is barely touching, and a girl singing from the bottom of a well.

She takes the side facing the archway. He takes the window, and sets Gloria’s box against the wall beside the napkins. Bev comes with two heavy cups and a pot. “Two lemon meringue,” Skye tells her, “and coffee till we die. He’s paying.” Bev writes it down without comment and goes.

Within ten minutes Skye’s bare feet are up on his side of the booth, crossed at the ankle on the red leatherette by his hip, braided anklet and all. She came in off forty degrees of gravel with nothing on them. He touches the top of one with the back of his hand, to check, and it’s warm. The cold doesn’t seem to apply to her.

“How’s Marlene?” she asks, with a look at his eyebrow, once Bev is out of earshot. “Still in Erie,” he says. “He took her back.” “I’m still not buying it,” Skye says, and goes on with her coffee as if she has all the time in the world to wait for the real one.

The pie comes, two tall slices with the meringue browned into peaks. She picks up her fork, and before the first bite she looks once out the window beside him — at the black glass, the gravel, the trucks asleep in their rows under the lamps — and then she eats like she hasn’t since Sunday.

At the counter a minivan family is refueling on the way to somebody’s Thanksgiving: a father asleep sitting up with his cap over his eyes, a mother doing math on a napkin, a little boy under the stools, and a girl of about thirteen in pajama pants and a Hollister hoodie, who swivels around on her stool and stares into the back room with her mouth open. She tugs her mother’s sleeve and whispers. Her mother doesn’t look up from the napkin. Skye, still chewing, gives the girl a small wave with the fork hand, and the girl ducks behind her mother like she’s been shot at.
“So what was it?” he says. It’s a fair question; he’s been carrying it since Sunday. “The job.”
“A carpet,” she says. “A wall. A woman with pins in her mouth.”
“That’s three jobs.”
“It’s one job with three kinds of standing still.”
“Okay. What are you *in*?”

She looks at him over the heavy cup, taking her time about it, and he can see she’s enjoying this. Then she pulls a napkin out of the dispenser, takes a Sharpie out of the flannel’s pocket, uncaps it with her teeth, writes on the napkin in capitals, and turns it around and slides it across the table.

body.title: A napkin, the Starlite
body.text:

“So she’s me.”
“So she’s *me*.” She taps the napkin with the Sharpie. “You’re the Bible salesman. Go.”
“I don’t —”
“You do one voice. I was there. Tonight you do two.” She pushes Gloria’s box across the table at him, string and all. “That’s your sample case.”
Mazzy Star goes on being underwater. Skye folds her hands on the Formica, a philosopher with a wooden leg and no time for salesmen, and waits for hers.

response: He stands up. That’s the first thing — he gets up out of the booth of a truck stop on the 101 and takes off a hat he isn’t wearing and holds it over his heart, and lifts Gloria’s box by the string like a valise full of Scripture, and what comes out of his mouth is from three states south of anywhere he has ever been. He’s just a country boy, ma’am. He’s selling Bibles. He could tell from the road she was real good country people, and he’s come to speak of serious things. He sits down on the edge of her side of the booth, uninvited. He calls her ma’am eleven times. He turns the hat around and around by its brim.

He’s good. Neither of them saw it coming, him least of all, and for most of a minute he forgets to be embarrassed. Hulga runs out of lines before he does. Skye sits there with her mouth a little open, and then she caps the Sharpie and says, “There’s a second voice in there. I *knew* it.”

body: By five past two the minivan family has paid and gone. Crossing the gravel, the girl in pajama pants walks backward to the van so she can keep looking at the window, and her mother steers her by the hood. Bev comes through the archway with the pot, tops up both their cups, and goes back to her truckers.
“You know,” Jack says, “if you ever get on TV, I’ll buy one. Just to watch.”

Skye laughs into her coffee. It goes everywhere — the cup, the saucer, the front of the flannel — and the trucker nearest the archway turns around on his stool to see what happened back there. She waves a napkin at him: nothing, sorry, carry on. “Deal,” she says, mopping. “*Deal*.” She doesn’t explain. Jack decides it’s two in the morning, and at two in the morning everything is a little funny.
She nods at the box against the wall. “Tell me about the pie.”
“It isn’t mine. It’s for my grandmother.” He says the next part to the box against the wall. “She fell on Monday.”
She stops eating to listen, and he tells her.

response: He tells her all of it. The Hollis steps, and Gina’s text with no capitals and the word *ambulance* in the middle of it. The stairs his grandmother had been keeping off for two weeks, sleeping in her chair in the front room so she wouldn’t have to climb them, and went up on Monday anyway, for her good rosary, because she’d decided God could tell the difference, and came down the fast way. His sister finding her. St. Elizabeth’s. A broken wrist, six stitches over the eye, and a monitor on her heart because of the dizzy spells; they’re keeping her for that.
“And my dad drove her.” She hears that, and that’s all he gives her of it.
She listens the way she listened in the car on Friday, chin down, and when he runs out she reaches across and takes a swallow of his coffee instead of saying anything.

Skye takes the facts one at a time and sets them out on the table in front of her like she’s going to need them later.

body: “Tell me about her,” Skye says. “Not the fall. *Her*.”

She leans in on her elbows with the fork still in her hand and turns every bit of herself toward him, and he gets the feeling of the lights in a room being adjusted, one at a time, until the only one left on is the one on him.

So he tells her. Carmela Rinaldi, eighty-four, from San Giovanni in Fiore, up in the mountains in Calabria, where the winters are worse than Youngstown’s — she says it like a boast. Came over in 1951 with one suitcase. The rosary every night in Calabrese, which is not Italian, she’ll tell you, and which the saints understand better. Cardoons at every holiday, battered and fried, which nobody in the house likes and everybody eats. A twenty folded small and pressed into his palm at the door every time he leaves, with a look that means don’t tell your mother. The chair by the front window, where she says the beads and keeps an eye on Glenwood Avenue to see who isn’t going to Mass.
“She calls me Giacomino,” he says. “And every phone call, she asks the same thing. *E la ragazza?*”
“What’s that?”
“‘And the girl?’”
“Which girl?”
He picks up his coffee.

Skye watches him drink it. “Right,” she says. “The one who’s seeing somebody.” She doesn’t make it a question, and she moves on without a ripple: what is a cardoon, actually, botanically, because she has been nodding at the word for five minutes and has no idea. A thistle, he tells her. You eat the stalks. She looks at him as if he has confessed to a crime in a foreign country and she’d like to visit.

“I could do her,” she says. “Give me a line. How does she say *ragazza*?” And she has already started — the shoulders coming down and in, one hand going up to settle a kerchief that isn’t there, the chin lifting toward a window on a street she has never seen —
Then she sets her fork down on the plate.
“No,” she says. “I’m not doing her. She’s yours.”
She turns the fork over, tines down, and looks at it.
“I’m named for a grandmother I met twice,” she says. “She sent me a holy card every birthday till I was nine. Saints. Gold around the edges. I don’t have any of them.”
Then she picks the fork back up and takes the last of the meringue off his plate with it. “When do you go?”
“Today. In about five hours. With my roommate.”
“Good,” she says, as if that settles the roommate, and goes straight on. “Five hours. Give me Thanksgiving. Give me the table. Who sits where.”

He gives her the table on Glenwood Avenue: his father at the end by the kitchen door, his mother never sitting down, Nonna at the corner where she can reach everything and correct everyone, his sisters, and this year an extra chair. She wants to know what’s on it. She wants to know who carves. She wants to know if anybody cries, and when he says his mother, at grace, every year, she nods like that was the right answer.
“What about you?”

“My mother’s,” Skye says. “There’ll be a lot of people I don’t know, and all of them will be very interested in how I’m doing. Nineteen years old, and somebody will still ask me if I’m eating.” She smiles when she says it, a smile with a good many teeth in it, and pours more sugar into a coffee that already has plenty.
At five to three Bev comes around again with the pot, and this time she stops with it over Skye’s cup and doesn’t pour. She studies Skye over the top of her reading glasses.
“Anybody ever tell you you look like somebody?”
“Everybody looks like somebody, Bev,” Skye says, sweet as anything.
Bev weighs that, pours, and takes the pot back up front.
It’s a good line. Jack would like to have it.
Skye watches her go, and wraps both hands around the heavy cup and looks at him across the table.
“Can I ask you something?”
“You’ve been asking me things for an hour and a half.”
“Something I want to know.” She works out how to put it. “Not the argument. I can do the argument — you did it in the window on Friday, it was very good. What’s it *like*? Believing. On a Tuesday.”
He opens his mouth and doesn’t have it ready.

“I do yoga,” she says, to help. “There’s a part at the end, savasana — you lie on your back on the floor with your palms up like you’re dead, it’s actually called corpse pose — and the teacher walks around in her socks and says, *You are exactly where you need to be.* And every single time, for about one breath, I believe her.” She thinks about it. “Then I think about my car.”
“Corpse pose,” Jack says, delighted.
“It’s very restful. And the philosophy part I get. The First Mover. Somebody had to start it. Something can’t come out of nothing — that’s a plot problem. That’s just a good writers’ room.”

She tips her head at him. “On the beach you said most nights nobody answers, and you go anyway.” She taps the rim of the cup with her fork. “I keep thinking about that. It’s a terrible business plan.”
“On a Tuesday,” Jack says, slowly, because he wants to get it right for her, “mostly it’s a Hail Mary in the shower when I can’t think —”
“Hail Mary, full of grace,” Skye says.

He stops. She doesn’t — “the Lord is with thee” — and he goes with her, because he can’t not; he has been saying it with whoever starts it since before he could tie his shoes. So they say the first half together across a booth in a truck stop at three in the morning, low, under the jukebox: *Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb, Jesus.* She has every word, and every word in its place, and every one of them a little careful, set down by itself, none of the run-together of a kid who learned it kneeling at a wake. She stops at the Holy Name like it’s the end of her line.
“For a role,” she says. “Forty takes. A chapel.”
“What were you playing?”
“A nice girl.”

He laughs. She is so pleased with herself for knowing it, and she is so close — she has the words, every one, better than half the Newman Center — and he wants to give her the rest of it, the half that asks for something, *now and at the hour of our death*, and he doesn’t know how you hand that to somebody across a table. He looks at the cup and doesn’t drink from it. Under the table her bare feet find his shin and settle there, and she waits for him to tell her what it’s like.

response: “Like being known,” Jack says. “All of it. Even the parts you’d cut. And not getting thrown out.”
She takes that in slowly, her thumb going around the rim of the cup.
Then her face clears, like somebody who has found the door. “So it’s like acting,” she says. “You do it long enough, and it becomes true.”
“It’s the other way round,” Jack says. “It’s true first.”
“Is it?”

She isn’t arguing. She wants to know; she leans across the table to hear it. And he has a hundred ways to say it — Aquinas, Augustine, Newman, Nonna’s beads going through her fingers in the chair by the window — and not one of them will go across a booth. He holds the heavy cup in both hands. Her feet are warm against his shin. Out on the gravel the first of the trucks starts up, deep in its chest, and then another.
“Yeah,” he says. “It is.”
She nods slowly and, for once, doesn’t say anything back.

body: A trucker feeds a dollar into the jukebox on his way down the hall to the showers, a towel over his shoulder and a shaving kit under his arm, and he’s gone before his song comes on. It plays for the two of them instead: Merle Haggard, “Silver Wings,” a steel guitar and a man standing on a runway watching somebody leave.
“How are you getting home?” Skye says.
“Plane. One change. My dad’s meeting us in Pittsburgh.” He hears himself add the next part. “I’ve never been up.”
She stops with the cup halfway to her mouth. “Never?”
“My dad drove me out in August. In the truck.”
She puts the cup down. “Get the window,” she says. “Don’t blink. You only get the first one once.”
“That’s the advice?”
“That’s all of it. What do you do up there — do you pray?”
“I’ll pray.”
“For what?”
“That it stays up.”
“That’s just physics.”
“Then I’ll pray for physics.”
She laughs. Then she slides out of the booth, takes the heavy cup out of his hands, and sets it on the next table over, out of harm’s way.
“Up.”
“What for?”

“You’ve never been up, so you’re going to be the one who’s been up ten thousand times.” She points down the strip of linoleum between the booths, back toward the restrooms under a light that hums. “That’s the aisle. You’re the flight attendant. Twenty-two years in the air, your feet hurt, you’ve seen everything twice. I’m in twenty-two C.” She slides back in on his side, by the window, buckles a seat belt that isn’t there and pulls it tight across her lap with both hands, and when she looks up at him she’s somebody else: a woman of seventy in a church coat, on her way to a grandson in Tucson, with her purse on her knees and both hands locked on the handle of it, who has never in her life been higher than the second floor of the Sears in Bakersfield.
“Young man,” she says, in a voice gone thin and Baptist. “Is it supposed to make that noise?”

The noise is the Starlite’s ice machine dropping a load somewhere in the back. Jack stands in the aisle of a truck stop at twenty to four in the morning with nowhere to go but forward, and looks down at a frightened old woman in a red leatherette booth, and finds he knows what to say to her. He has been saying it to his grandmother since he was ten.

“That noise, ma’am, is the plane being glad to see you.” He takes the laminated menu out from behind the napkins. “If I could have your attention for the safety demonstration.” And he gives it, pointing with two fingers held together: the menu is the card in the seat-back pocket; the sugar pourer is the oxygen mask — *secure your own before assisting others* — and the exits are two, by the cassettes, and one through the kitchen, which the management would rather you didn’t use. In the unlikely event of a water landing, he tells her, her seat cushion may be used as a flotation device, and this one has been patched twice with red tape and will float as long as she needs it to.
“And if it doesn’t?”
“Then I come back for you, ma’am. That’s the job.”
The old woman looks up at him from twenty-two C with her hands still locked on a purse that isn’t there, and her chin trembles, exactly once. “You’re very kind,” she says. “Are you married?”
“I’m working, ma’am.”
“My granddaughter’s single. She’s a dental hygienist.” She pats the leatherette beside her. “Sit down. Tell me about your people.”
In the archway Bev has stopped with the pot to watch. “Life jackets are in back with the mops,” she tells the old woman. “He’s new.”

Skye puts her forehead down on the Formica and laughs into it, and the purse goes wherever the pins went. When she comes up, a pickup is pulling in under the lamps outside, and she watches it through the glass until the driver climbs down — a man in a feed cap, headed for the showers — and only then looks back at Jack, still standing in the aisle with the menu.
“You did that like you’ve done it,” she says.
“I’ve got a grandmother.”
He sits down beside her, where she patted. She reaches over and hands him back his coffee from the next table, and then she folds her hands around her own cup, and he watches her decide something.

“I want you to miss me,” she says. “Over Thanksgiving. A reasonable amount.” She says it the way she ordered the pie, as a thing a person might simply want and ask for, in a public place, with truckers. “Is that allowed?”
On Glenwood Avenue people want things for twenty years and die without mentioning it. She has mentioned it over lemon meringue at half past three in the morning, and now she is waiting to hear back.

body: She drives him back down the grade with the heater on and the tape turned low, and they don’t talk. He doesn’t want to, and she seems to have decided not to, and the twenty minutes are better for it.

The Anacapa lot at a quarter past four is dew on windshields and sodium light, and one of the lamps on the Lagoon side has a tick in it, a dry click every few seconds, like it’s keeping time for somebody. The moon went down hours ago. She pulls into the far row by the bike racks and turns the engine off, and the tape stops in the middle of a word.
In the quiet she turns in her seat to face him, one bare foot tucked up under her.
“I’m not going to ask this time,” she says. “Last time you didn’t let me get to the end of the sentence.”
“And I’m not doing the grandmother tonight. I retired her.”
Then she waits. She’s good at it. She pulls the other knee up, rests her chin on it, and keeps her eyes on him.

body: He’s the one who stops. He takes his mouth off hers and steps back half a step, not far; his forehead stays against hers, and both of them are breathing like they ran up the grade. Her hands are still inside his jacket.

She opens her eyes and looks at him from very close. She looks interested, and pleased, the way she looked at him across the napkin at the Starlite — like she has just watched him do a thing she wasn’t sure he could do, and liked the way he did it.
“Go home, Ohio,” she says. “You have a plane.”
She takes her hands back out of his Carhartt one at a time, and does up the top snap for him against the cold, and gets in. The window comes down a crack.
“Miss me a reasonable amount.”

Then the Saab backs out of the row and crosses the lot, the one taillight swinging red across the wet asphalt, and turns onto Ocean Road toward the 101. He listens to the Saab downshift for the on-ramp, and then the 101 has it.
She’s the one. She takes her mouth away, and when he leans after it she puts her thumb on his mouth, where hers was, and holds it there.

He stands still for it. Her thumb is warm and a little rough at the edge of the nail, and she keeps it at the corner of his mouth while she looks at him, like she wants to remember exactly where she left off. Then she steps back with her thumb still up between them, as if she could hold the place.

s20k.slug: WEDNESDAY · 4:20 AM · THE ANACAPA LOT, AGAINST THE SAAB
body: When he gets around the back of the car she’s leaning on the driver’s door in the green flannel with her bare feet on the cold asphalt and her hands in her pockets, waiting for him like there is no plane in the morning and never will be.
“Friday was fast,” she says. “I’ve been thinking about the slow way ever since.”
He comes in close enough that she has to tip her head back to look at him. She doesn’t take her hands out of her pockets. She makes him come the rest of the way.

For the first second her mouth is cool from the night air, and still. She doesn’t do anything with it, and neither does he. They stand in the orange light with their mouths just touching, and he can feel her breathing, and the cold, and his own heart going in his ears. Then she opens her mouth under his, slowly, and it starts.

She tastes of coffee and the lemon off the pie — on Friday it was salt — and she kisses the way she said she would, slow on purpose, every second of it something she has decided. When he goes faster she goes slower and makes him come back down to her. Her hands come out of the flannel and go inside his open Carhartt and lie flat against his shirt, over his ribs, warm through the cotton, and they stay there while his heart knocks against one of them.

He gets a hand into her hair. It’s dry tonight, and heavy, and it slides through his fingers and falls back against her neck, and he follows it down to the hinge of her jaw and holds her face there with his thumb along her cheekbone. Her jaw fits his palm like it was measured for it. He kisses the corner of her mouth, and then the place his thumb was, and then lower, the side of her throat where her pulse is going, and she tips her head back against the cold canvas of the top to give it to him and says something that isn’t a word. He comes back up to her mouth and she’s already there, open, waiting for him.

She takes him by the front of the Carhartt and pulls, and keeps on pulling, until there’s no air left anywhere along him that isn’t her — the door at her back, her hips against his, her knees, the cold flannel and the warm weight of her inside it. He is eighteen and he has wanted this since she put her feet up on his side of the booth, and his body is completely honest about it. Pressed against him like this she can’t help knowing. She doesn’t move away. She makes a low pleased sound into his mouth instead, and he feels it in the backs of his knees.

The cold is everywhere they aren’t touching: the back of his neck, the backs of his hands, his ears, his ankles where his jeans ride up. Everywhere they are, it’s gone. The lamp ticks over them. He stops counting the ticks; he stops knowing how long. A car goes by out on Ocean Road and its headlights swing across the two of them and keep going, and he doesn’t stop for it, and she doesn’t either.

Some part of him is keeping very exact track of his hands. One is in her hair. The other is open on the flannel at the small of her back, an inch above the waist of her cutoffs, where the shirt is warm all the way through from her and he could find the hem without looking. He keeps his hand on the flannel. He knows exactly where it is, and exactly where it isn’t, and why, the way you know where the edge of a roof is in the dark.

She feels him keep it there. He can tell, because she smiles against his mouth — the corner of her top lip going up under his — and kisses him harder, slow and harder, like she has found a game she likes and means to play it for a long time.
Somewhere in it she says his name, once, against his jaw, and then she goes back to his mouth, and he forgets to answer.
Her hands have closed in his shirt. She isn’t going to be the one, not yet; he can tell by how she’s holding on.

s21.slug: WEDNESDAY · 4:40 AM · THE ANACAPA LOT, THE CURB BY THE BIKE RACKS → ROOM 412
body: He sits down on the curb by the bike racks because his legs make a good case for it, with Gloria’s box on his knees. It’s twenty to five. The lot is dew and orange light, the eucalyptus along the Lagoon black against a sky that hasn’t started anything yet, and he sits there for forty minutes, and all forty of them are her mouth.

He goes through it from the beginning. The first second, before either of them moved: her mouth against his, cool from the air, not doing anything, and her breath going in and out against his upper lip. After that, the coffee and the lemon. The one chapped place, at the corner on the left, from the cold or from driving the 101 all fall with the top down — the one rough thing about her; he found it and she made a sound in her throat and didn’t mind. The freckle by her mouth that he only saw when she pulled back, under the lamp. The bow of her top lip, which comes to a small peak in the middle, like somebody drew it there to show you where to start.

The way that lip lifted when she smiled into it, so that he felt the smile before he could see anything — felt it go up against his mouth at the corner and knew she was pleased with him. How slow she was. How she would draw back until their mouths were barely touching, and wait there, and make him come the rest of the way, every time. That it was on purpose. That she’d been thinking about it since Friday, and told him so.

body: At some point he has the RAZR out. It’s open in his hand to SKYE (MISFIT), and his thumb is resting on the 5. He doesn’t press it. He closes the phone and holds it.
At some point his other hand has gone up to the St. Michael at his throat. It’s warm from him. He keeps hold of it.

He knows how it would go in the box on a Saturday — *Bless me, Father* — and the sentence after that, which would have her in it, and *four days*, and *I wanted* — and he lets the sentence stop there, because he isn’t in the box. He’s on a curb with a pie. Her mouth is still on his, more or less. He can feel exactly where.
At twenty past five the sprinklers along the Lagoon path come on all at once, hissing, and one of them gets the curb. He takes the hint.

In 412 Theo is sitting up in bed in the navy robe with his iPhone in his lap and an alarm set for half past five that he isn’t going to need. He watches Jack come in and sit down on his own bed in the Carhartt with the pie box on his knees, and he looks confused again, the way he looked at six on Saturday, and his eyes go from the pie box to the clock to Jack’s boots before he says anything.
“Did you sleep?”
“No.”
“Doing what?” Theo says. “Another book?”

journal.title: Skye
journal.text: Skye. No last name — she said *Out*. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Doesn’t go here. Not yet, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. I was the one who stopped.
