body: Theo drove, with the top up for once, and Gloria’s box rode on Jack’s knees from the Anacapa lot to the airport with its string knotted twice. The coast was still black on the right when they started. Somewhere down the empty stretch of it the hills came apart from the sky — a line first, then a ridge, then a ridge with oaks on it — and Jack watched it happen with the lemon still at the corner of his mouth, all the way through Goleta. Theo drove with both hands and the radio off.

Now the SL sits in long-term parking, nose out, between a minivan and a Suburban, like a dare. The terminal is white stucco and red tile, built for some other decade’s idea of how many people fly, and on the Wednesday before Thanksgiving the line goes out the door and down the sidewalk: car seats, a soldier, a girl with a cello case, a man checking a turkey fryer in its original box.

Julian’s car is at the curb with its flashers going. Lena gets out in the cardigan with a duffel and a box of Kleenex, and Julian comes around and lifts her bag out of the trunk and sets it on the curb, and that’s as far as he’s allowed; a man in an orange vest is already waving the next car up.
Theo, passing him with the boarding passes fanned in one hand, says, “Julian. Don’t write a song about the drive back.”
Julian smiles at the pavement. Jack, holding a pie, is in no position to stop anybody.
Lena looks at Theo’s bag — a leather weekender with somebody else’s initials on it — and at Jack. “Theo Vance is going to *Youngstown*?”
“I’ve been invited,” Theo says. “I intend to be a revelation.”
She looks from one of them to the other. Then she hands Theo her Kleenex to carry, as the price of the information.

The security line is shoes off and three ounces of anything in a quart bag. Lena stands behind Jack in her socks with her boots in one hand, the Justins, resoled twice, and goes around tomorrow’s table on Dupre Street for him chair by chair: Daddy carving, Josie biting somebody, her mother counting the chairs twice. She skips one chair. He lets her.
At the belt the pie goes through the X-ray in its white box between Jack’s boots and Lena’s, and the woman at the screen stops the belt and studies it for some time. “What kind?”
“Diplomatic,” says Theo, in his socks.
While the woman decides, Lena’s hand comes to rest on the steel rail beside his, an inch off, and neither of them moves it.

Past the checkpoint it’s one long room for everybody, the gates along the windows and the planes right out there on the apron with stairs rolled up to them, near enough to watch a pilot drink his coffee. Lena sits on her duffel and digs in her bag past her worship aid and a library book, and hands up a holy card: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, blue and gold, the Child on her arm, one corner bent. “For your nonna. She’s a New Orleans saint. She works fast.” On the back, in red, Lena has written *Carmela Rinaldi* and *St. Bernard’s, Breaux Bridge — O. Broussard*, so the saint will know who sent her.
Then she looks up at him properly, the first time this morning, and takes her time about it. “You look like you didn’t sleep.”
“I didn’t.”

She reaches up and taps the card in his hand, twice, on the saint. “Tell her it’s urgent. She likes urgent.” She sits back on the duffel. “Call me Thursday. After the pie. I want to hear Theo say *pop*.”
“I’ve been practicing,” Theo says.

Becca is at the next gate — Seattle, then Spokane — sitting on the carpet with her back against a pillar and her planner open on her knees, and when she sees him she’s up off the floor in one move. “You’re *flying*!”

Theo is perfect to her. He holds her coffee level while she goes through her bag, gives it back without a drop gone, and asks after Idaho as if it were a relative. What she finds is a holy card: St. Raphael, with his staff and his fish, walking a boy down a road.
“For your grandmother,” Becca says. “When Father Osei said Youngstown, I knew. I’m still allowed to pray for her, right?”
“You’re allowed,” Jack says.
“I’m telling Mom at the table tomorrow,” she says. “Then Facebook.”
Then her eyes go past his shoulder, across the gate area, to Lena on her duffel with her boarding pass in her lap, and Becca watches her and says nothing at all.
The RAZR rides in his shirt pocket the entire time she talks, and keeps quiet.

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait. Stuck on the touch tank all weekend while we were at Big Sur: the weekend volunteer has the swine flu. Asked me for the monks’ fruitcake for her Grandma Agnes — the only honest fruitcake in America. I handed in my homework six days early. St. Isidore and St. Maria: her first. Early, she said. Nobody’s early but her. Halloween: she sewed my costume out of a Rathdrum Feed & Seed sack. She was St. Maria de la Cabeza in Mrs. Fitch’s lace, with a water jug. Best Saint, by acclamation — a gold halo. Never won anything that wasn’t a heifer. Home at 11:40 for the six o’clock tank; the volunteer still has the flu. ‘Farmer.’ Theo’s birthday: huckleberry jam from her mother, for Theo — the Idaho gift. Next to his mother all night. ‘He’s *mine*. Since the beach cleanup.’ Toasted St. Martin de Porres: a dog and a cat and a mouse, one bowl. The Portolá steps, November 4th: her mom’s been calling me her boyfriend since September. She asked if she could tell her she’s right. I said yes. Her mom first, then Facebook. She flies home to Spokane the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Her mother has named the turkey. She asked how I’m getting home. Greyhound. She frowned. Her mother sent a box: socks, cookies, two jars of huckleberry — JACK, and FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE. She offered me Daisy’s money. Six hundred and twelve dollars. It’s there, she says. Daisy doesn’t mind. Saturday, Ohio State in overtime: she gave me a photograph of the elephant seals in a frame she painted, every seal labeled with what it weighs. She’ll call during her dad’s grace on Thanksgiving so I can hear it. She wants to watch Michigan here, with me. ‘Someday I want to see your house. Is that okay to say?’ Ma wrote her. Three days after Christmas. Pittsburgh’s cheaper than Cleveland. She looked. Wednesday, in Eli’s truck, I told her. She said she did everything right, and she did. ‘It just isn’t the thing, is it.’ She asked me to leave it up on Facebook till she’s told her mom at the table. Thursday at two she texted. Still praying for me — not a girlfriend thing, she says. At the twelve-ten she turned around across the aisle at the sign of peace and held out her hand. Then she held it out to Lena. At the airport, a week to the day: St. Raphael, for Nonna. Father Osei read the name at the twelve-ten, and she heard.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast.

s24.slug: WEDNESDAY · 12:20 PM · DENVER INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT, CONCOURSE B
body: The PA in Concourse B is a woman who never gets to finish a sentence before another woman starts one on top of her — a gate change, a final call for Omaha, a reminder that unattended bags will be — and under her the rolling bags go by in both directions, wheels thumping over every seam in the floor.

The connection is forty minutes late, and the board has stopped pretending otherwise. Every outlet on the concourse has somebody’s cord in it and somebody sitting guard. His own Dell is at the bottom of the duffel with its eleven minutes of battery, and it can stay there. Jack is on the carpet with his back against a pillar and Gloria’s box upright beside him.

Theo is across the concourse, up on a shoeshine stand — a high leather chair on a platform, brass rests for the feet — with his iPhone to his ear and his loafers in the hands of a man in a canvas apron. “Poppy,” he said, going over. “She’s choosing between our parents and wants a consultant.” Whatever she’s saying now, Theo laughs at it with his head back.

body: Her last name comes to him on the floor of an airport in the middle of the country. Callender. Two Ls. He tries it under his breath with the first name in front of it, and it sounds like a girl he hasn’t met yet.

Somewhere on Facebook there is a request with his name on it, waiting for Confirm or Ignore, and her picture beside it, and he can’t get to either one. The RAZR doesn’t do the internet, not on his plan; it barely does Denver. The Dell is dead weight. Theo’s iPhone does the internet, thirty feet away, and Jack would sooner walk to Pittsburgh. Sitting there, he notices something he hasn’t noticed in five days: he doesn’t have a single picture of her.
The RAZR rings in his hand. GINA.
“Ma says are you in Denver,” Gina says, no hello. Under her voice there are keys going, fast — the basement, the family Dell, where she lives when school is out. “Ma says is Theo eating. Ma says —”
“I’m in Denver.” Across the concourse Theo is pointing out to the shoeshine man a place on the left loafer that still needs him. “He’s eating.”
“Ma’s at St. Elizabeth’s. Nonna told the nurse she doesn’t need a monitor, she’s from Calabria. Dad’s been ready for the airport since *noon*.”
Jack looks at the little screen of the phone, and then across the concourse at Theo, with a stranger shining his shoes and his sister in his ear.

s24a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 12:24 PM · DENVER INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT, CONCOURSE B
body: The keys stop.
“Oh my God,” Gina says.
Then, loud enough to come out of a RAZR held tight to his ear: “JACK. SHE’S ON TV.”

A woman three seats down, rocking a stroller with her foot, looks over at him. Across the concourse the PA is talking over itself about Omaha, and Theo, up on the stand with his eyes shut and Poppy in his ear, is letting the man work.

“She’s *Cassidy*. On *Sweetwater*. Thursdays at nine — everybody at Ursuline watches it, Jack, *everybody*, Kelsey has the song from it on her phone — she’s the *nice* one. She’s the one everybody protects. There’s two of her. There’s her, and then there’s her *fan page*, with *fans* — it doesn’t even say friends, Jack, it says *fans*, and there’s *thousands*. She’s *so pretty*. Like TV pretty. Because she’s *on TV*. There’s a picture of her on a *dock*, in a *blazer*, with like six other girls in blazers, and she’s in the middle looking like she’d say sorry to a *chair*.” She goes for a breath and doesn’t get one. “How do you — where did you — you don’t even *have* a TV.”
*— it’s Cassidy, I swear to God —*
*People get me confused with a girl.* *What girl?* *A nice one.*

He told a girl who is on television Thursdays at nine that he doesn’t own a television, so it wouldn’t mean anything. To put her at ease. Then he explained General Motors to her. In her own car. With dates. And she let him. She drove up the 101 with one bare foot on the gas and asked him about Lordstown like he was the one in the car worth hearing about.

Jack slides down the pillar until he is lying flat on the carpet of Concourse B, with the phone at his ear and Gloria’s box standing over him. The woman with the stroller wheels it a few feet farther off.
“Jack. *Jack*. Where did you *meet* her?”
“At a party. Over a book.”
“Of *course* over a book. What did you *do*.”
“We had coffee.”
“*JACK*.”
Gina, at a lower volume: “Is she nice? Like in real life. Is she the nice one?”
Jack, on his back on the carpet, sees her to the waist in the Pacific in a man’s flannel in November, swearing through her teeth.
“No,” he says. “Not like that.”
“Oh my *God*.” The keys again, furious. “Kelsey is going to *die* —”
“Kelsey’s not going to anything.”
“Also your Facebook still says you’re in a relationship. With *Idaho*.” “She asked me to leave it up till she tells her mom.” “That’s so nice,” Gina says, “I’m mad about it.”
He sits up. Theo has switched feet on the stand.
“G. Nobody. Not Ma. Not Pop. Not Nonna. Not Danny. Not Theo.”
“Danny calls *tonight*. Who’s — the rich one? I’ve never even *met* the rich one.”
“Nobody.”
Down the line the keys go again, slower, a few at a time, and quit.
“Not even the nun?”
“Lena’s got a boyfriend, G.”
“I know. The one with the cardigans. She’s in his pictures.” One key. “That’s not what I asked.”
Then, through the basement window and down the line, the Silverado’s horn in the driveway — one long, two short, the way their father has called people out to the truck since before Gina was born.

“Dad wants me to come look at the truck. He *washed* it. In *November*. For the *rich one*.” The horn again. “I have to go. Jack.” She brings her voice down to what she must think is a whisper. “*On TV*.”
Click.
He sits on the carpet with the phone in his lap. The PA wants a passenger named Ruiz at the white courtesy phone. He opens the RAZR to SKYE (MISFIT) and puts his thumb on the keys.

body: Theo comes back across the concourse with his loafers shining and drops into the seat beside the pillar. He holds one foot out for Jack to admire. “A man named Curtis,” he says, “has restored my faith in Denver. I told him where I was going, and he gave me the good polish out of sympathy.” Then he looks down at Jack on the carpet, with the phone shut in his fist.
“What?”
“Nothing.”
Theo crosses his ankles and turns his attention to the other shoe.

They board families with small children first, and the woman with the stroller goes past him to the jetway giving him a wide berth. After them, group three. The phone buzzes in Jack’s hand from the gate to the end of the jetway, faster than T9 was ever built to answer. She wants to know what Gina looks like (*like me. shed win*). What the scream sounded like (*the fire alarm at 3am*). Whether the pie made it through Denver (*under a seat. its fine*). How many people know (*one. and the stroller*). She wants to know everything at once, and she types the way she drives.

At the door of the plane the flight attendant looks at the phone, and then at him. He turns it off with her last one still lit on the screen — *go. ill still be on tv when you land* — and puts it in his shirt pocket, behind the two saints.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Doesn’t go here. Not yet, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. I was the one who stopped. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Saw Becca on my profile. Says she’s always wanted to play the other woman.
